stem: **Kaizen** is best described as

options.content: continuous improvement in small steps
options.rationale: Correct: every employee looks constantly for small improvements.

options.content: a once-a-year review by managers
options.rationale: Kaizen is constant and involves all employees, not an annual review by managers.

options.content: a way of delivering materials on time
options.rationale: That describes just-in-time, not kaizen.

options.content: a team that makes a whole product
options.rationale: That describes cell production.

explanation: Kaizen is the Japanese word for continuous improvement, achieved by many small changes suggested by workers.

stem: In **cell production**, workers are organised so that

options.content: a small team makes a whole product or part
options.rationale: Correct: the team takes responsibility for the whole job and for its quality.

options.content: each worker repeats one task all day
options.rationale: That describes a conventional flow line, which cells replace.

options.content: products are made only after orders arrive
options.rationale: That describes just-in-time production rather than cells.

options.content: design and production happen at the same time
options.rationale: That describes simultaneous engineering.

explanation: A cell is a small team making a complete product or component, so faults are found sooner and workers take responsibility.

stem: Which effect on **inventory** is most directly linked to just-in-time manufacturing?

options.content: Larger buffer stocks protect against delay
options.rationale: That is the opposite of JIT, which removes buffer stock.

options.content: Stock is checked once a year
options.rationale: JIT depends on constant, close control of stock, not an annual check.

options.content: Stock of materials is kept very low
options.rationale: Correct: materials arrive when they are needed, so little is stored.

options.content: Finished goods are made in advance of orders
options.rationale: JIT makes goods to meet orders rather than for stock.

explanation: JIT keeps stock of materials and finished goods to a minimum, which cuts storage cost and frees cash.
hints: JIT means materials arrive only when needed.

stem: A fictional furniture maker in Bulawayo changes to JIT delivery of timber. Which problem is **most likely** to cause production to stop?

options.content: Too much timber is stored in the yard
options.rationale: JIT removes large stores, so this is unlikely.

options.content: A supplier's delivery arrives late
options.rationale: Correct: with no buffer stock, a late delivery leaves workers without timber.

options.content: Workers make suggestions for improvement
options.rationale: Suggestions do not stop production.

options.content: The factory has too many finished chairs
options.rationale: JIT makes goods to order, so a pile of finished chairs is unlikely.

explanation: JIT removes the buffer of stock, so the business depends on reliable suppliers. A late delivery can stop production.
hints: What protects the firm when something goes wrong with supply?

stem: A fictional bakery in Masvingo employs 30 bakers. After introducing cell production its output rises from 9,000 loaves a month to 11,250 loaves a month with the same number of bakers. By what percentage has output per worker risen?

options.rationale: That takes the rise of 2,250 as a percentage of the new output (11,250).
That is the new output per worker, not the percentage change.
That is the rise in loaves, not a percentage.
Correct: output per worker rose from 300 to 375, an increase of 75 on 300.

explanation: Output per worker = 9,000 ÷ 30 = 300 before and 11,250 ÷ 30 = 375 after. Percentage rise = (375 - 300) ÷ 300 × 100 = 25%. Using the new figure as the base gives 20%.
hints: Work out the output per worker before and after.

stem: A fictional small shop in Chinhoyi sells bread whose demand is very uneven from day to day, and its flour supplier is unreliable. Which is the best reason why full JIT is **unlikely to suit it**?

options.content: Lean production always raises costs
options.rationale: Lean production normally lowers costs; the problem is the shop's conditions.

options.content: Workers cannot make suggestions in a shop
options.rationale: Workers can make suggestions in any business.

options.content: JIT works only for large businesses
options.rationale: Size alone does not decide whether JIT is suitable.

options.content: Uneven demand and unreliable supply
options.rationale: Correct: with no buffer stock, either factor could leave the shop without bread to sell.

explanation: JIT works best where demand is steady and suppliers are reliable. The shop has neither, so removing stock would risk lost sales.
hints: JIT depends on forecasting demand and receiving supplies on time.

stem: A quality circle is a group of workers who meet to find solutions to quality problems.
explanation: True. Quality circles are small groups from one work area who identify the causes of problems and suggest solutions to management.

stem: Lean production always increases a business's capacity to meet a sudden rise in demand.
explanation: False. Lean production removes spare capacity and buffer stock, so it can make it harder to meet a sudden rise in demand.

stem: Match each technique to its description.

right.content: A small team makes a whole product
Design and production work at the same time
A group of workers who meet to solve quality problems

explanation: Each technique is a different part of lean production.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: Lean production aims to remove {{blank:a}} while keeping quality. Just-in-time manufacturing keeps {{blank:b}} to a minimum.

explanation: Lean production removes waste; JIT keeps stock low.

stem: State **one** risk of using just-in-time manufacturing.
explanation: Accept any risk caused by having no buffer stock: late or failed deliveries, stoppage of production or inability to meet a sudden rise in orders.

stem: A fictional garment factory in Gweru made 15,000 garments in a month, of which 180 were defective after it introduced quality circles. Calculate the defect rate, to one decimal place. (Defect rate = defective garments ÷ output × 100.)
explanation: 180 ÷ 15,000 × 100 = 1.2%. Dividing output by the defects (15,000 ÷ 180) turns the fraction upside down and gives 83.3; 12% comes from dropping a zero.
workedSolution: 1. 180 ÷ 15,000 × 100 = 1.2%. Dividing output by the defects (15,000 ÷ 180) turns the fraction upside down and gives 83.3; 12% comes from dropping a zero.
hints: Divide the defective garments by the total output.

stem: A fictional hardware shop in Harare reduces its average stock from US\$30,000 to US\$11,000 after adopting just-in-time ordering. It assumes that holding stock costs 15% of its value each year. Calculate the annual saving in holding costs.
explanation: Fall in stock = 30,000 - 11,000 = US\$19,000. Saving = 19,000 × 15% = US\$2,850 a year. The US\$19,000 itself is cash released, not an annual saving.
workedSolution:
1. Fall in average stock = 30,000 - 11,000 = US\$19,000.
2. Annual holding-cost saving = 19,000 × 0.15 = US\$2,850.
hints: Find the fall in stock first, then take 15% of it.

stem: A fictional furniture workshop in Mutare spent US\$24,000 on labour and materials in a month and made 800 chairs. After a kaizen programme it spent US\$21,000 and made 840 chairs. Calculate the fall in cost per chair.
explanation: Before: 24,000 ÷ 800 = US\$30. After: 21,000 ÷ 840 = US\$25. The fall is US\$5 per chair. The fall in total cost (US\$3,000) is not the fall per chair.
workedSolution:
1. Cost per chair before = 24,000 ÷ 800 = US\$30.
2. Cost per chair after = 21,000 ÷ 840 = US\$25.
3. Fall = 30 - 25 = US\$5.
hints: Cost per chair = total cost ÷ number of chairs, before and after.

stem: Explain what is meant by waste in lean production.

points.description: Anything that uses resources but adds no value the customer would pay for
Examples: excess stock, waiting time, defects or overproduction
Lean production aims to find and remove it

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Waste is anything that uses resources but adds no value the customer would pay for, such as excess stock, waiting time, defects or overproduction. Lean production aims to find and remove it.

explanation: One point per mark.
hints: Think of what the customer is willing to pay for.

stem: A fictional tuck-shop supplier in Masvingo introduces a quality circle among its packers. Explain two benefits to the business.

points.description: Packers know the job and can spot the causes of errors
Application: fewer wrong or damaged orders reach the shops
Workers are more involved and motivated by being listened to
Application: lower labour turnover or better teamwork among the packers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The packers know the job well and can spot why orders are wrong or damaged, so fewer faulty orders reach the shops. Being listened to also motivates the packers, which can reduce labour turnover and improve teamwork.

explanation: Two benefits, each developed in context.
hints: Link each benefit to the packers or the shops.

stem: Analyse how cell production might affect the employees of a clothing factory.

points.description: Workers become multi-skilled because they do many tasks in the cell
Teamwork and responsibility for quality increase
Possible motivation gain from a more varied job
Training costs and worries about job loss or stress may arise

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In a cell, workers become multi-skilled because they carry out many tasks, and they share responsibility for quality. This can be more motivating than one repeated task. However, workers need training, and some may worry about job loss or feel more stress from team targets.

explanation: One point per mark.
hints: Consider both positive and negative effects for the workers.

stem: A fictional bakery chain in Bulawayo wants to adopt lean production in all its bakeries. Assess whether this is a good decision.

points.description: Waste, defects and stock can be reduced, which lowers cost
Kaizen and quality circles use the bakers' ideas and improve motivation
JIT needs reliable flour deliveries; late deliveries could stop baking
Demand for bread may rise sharply at certain times, and lean production leaves little spare capacity
Counter-argument: parts of lean production, such as kaizen, carry little risk and can be adopted anyway
Judgement with a reason, for example adopt kaizen now and JIT only where suppliers are reliable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Lean production could lower costs by cutting waste, defects and stock, and kaizen and quality circles would use the bakers' ideas and improve motivation. However, JIT depends on reliable flour deliveries, and a late delivery would stop baking, while sudden peaks in demand are harder to meet when there is little spare capacity. Kaizen carries little risk and could be adopted everywhere. The chain should adopt kaizen now and introduce JIT only in bakeries with reliable suppliers.

explanation: One point per mark; a judgement needs a reason.
hints: Separate the techniques: some carry little risk, others a lot.

stem: A fictional shoe factory in Gweru employs 24 workers. Before it introduced cell production it made 7,200 pairs of shoes a month. After the change, with the same workers, it made 8,640 pairs a month. Workers in each cell now check each pair for faults before passing it on.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate output per worker before the change.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage rise in output per worker after the change, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: After = 8,640 ÷ 24 = 360. Rise = (360 - 300) ÷ 300 × 100 = 20.0%. Using the new figure as the base gives 16.7%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. After = 8,640 ÷ 24 = 360. Rise = (360 - 300) ÷ 300 × 100 = 20.0%. Using the new figure as the base gives 16.7%.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain two ways in which cell production could help the factory to improve quality.

points.description: Each cell checks its own work, so faults are found at once
Application: faulty shoes are corrected before they pass to the next stage
Workers take responsibility for the whole product
Application: a cell that makes a faulty pair can see its own mistakes, so it has a reason to avoid them
Fewer defective shoes reach customers, protecting the factory's reputation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Each cell checks its own work, so a faulty pair of shoes is found and corrected at once before it moves on. The workers also take responsibility for the whole pair, so they have a reason to avoid mistakes. Fewer defective shoes reach customers, which protects the factory's reputation.

parts.explanation: Two ways, developed with the shoe factory.

explanation: Productivity 300 to 360 pairs per worker, a rise of 20.0%; cells improve quality by quick checking and shared responsibility.
hints: Percentage change uses the old figure as the base.

stem: A fictional mining-supplies manufacturer in Bulawayo introduced just-in-time delivery of steel and a kaizen scheme. Its average stock of steel fell from US\$36,000 to US\$14,000. It assumes that holding stock costs 20% of its value a year. The change cost US\$6,000 in training and new storage racks, paid in the first year. In the second year a lorry strike delayed deliveries and production stopped for three days.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the annual saving in holding costs.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Fall in average stock = 36,000 - 14,000 = US\$22,000.
2. Saving = 22,000 × 0.20 = US\$4,400 a year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate by how much the first-year cost of the change exceeds the first-year saving.
parts.explanation: 6,000 - 4,400 = US\$1,600, so the change makes a net loss of US\$1,600 in the first year.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 6,000 - 4,400 = US\$1,600, so the change makes a net loss of US\$1,600 in the first year.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain one reason why a lorry strike creates a problem for a business using just-in-time delivery.

points.description: There is no buffer stock of steel
Application: production stopped for three days
Workers are idle and orders may be late, so customers may be lost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The factory holds no buffer stock of steel, so when deliveries stopped production stopped for three days. Workers were idle and orders were late, so customers might look elsewhere.

parts.explanation: A reason developed using the case.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the manufacturer was right to introduce just-in-time delivery.

points.description: Holding costs fall by US\$4,400 a year and cash is released
The first-year cost of US\$6,000 means it takes more than one year to recover
Risk: the three-day stoppage cost output and goodwill
Kaizen may reduce waste and improve quality in addition
Counter-argument: a small buffer stock could protect against the strike without losing most of the saving
Judgement with a reason, for example worthwhile over several years if some stock is held as a safeguard

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The change saves US\$4,400 a year and releases US\$22,000 of cash, but its first-year cost of US\$6,000 means the manufacturer takes more than a year to recover the outlay. The three-day stoppage shows the risk of holding no buffer. Kaizen may add savings by reducing waste. Overall the decision was right over several years, provided the firm now holds a small safety stock of steel to protect against strikes and late deliveries.

parts.explanation: Weighs the saving, the cost and the risk of stoppage to a judgement.
hints: Compare the saving, the cost and the risk.

explanation: Saving US\$4,400 a year; first-year net loss US\$1,600; JIT risks stoppage without a buffer.
hints: Holding-cost saving = fall in stock × the percentage.
A negative net result is a loss.

stem: A fictional school production unit near Harare makes uniforms. Orders are steady during the school terms and very low during holidays. It buys cloth from two suppliers in Harare who always deliver within a day. The head of the unit is considering lean production: cell production for sewing, JIT delivery of cloth and a monthly kaizen meeting with all staff. There are 12 staff, most of them pupils on work experience who join for one term.

points.description: A system where materials arrive only when needed for production
Finished goods are made to meet orders
So that very little stock is held

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Just-in-time is a system in which materials arrive only when they are needed and goods are made to meet orders, so that very little stock is held.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse one reason why JIT could suit the unit.

points.description: Suppliers are reliable and deliver within a day
Stock of cloth can be cut, so storage space and cash tied up fall
Application: orders are steady in term, so cloth needs can be forecast
Waste from cloth that is not used falls or spoils

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The two suppliers deliver within a day, so the unit can safely order cloth when it is needed. Orders are steady during term, so the amount of cloth needed can be forecast, and cutting stock frees storage space and cash.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the unit should adopt lean production.

points.description: JIT and cell production suit steady orders and reliable suppliers
Kaizen needs trained staff who stay long enough to suggest and test ideas; pupils stay for one term only
Low demand in holidays means little need for spare capacity, so lean working carries little risk
Training and reorganising the sewing room cost money and time for a small unit
Counter-argument: pupils' fresh ideas may help and the method is a useful lesson in business
Judgement with a reason: adopt JIT and cells, and make the kaizen meeting simple

levels.descriptor: Techniques linked to the unit's conditions, both benefits and limits weighed, and a justified judgement
Benefits and limits with some application; judgement weakly supported
Describes lean techniques with little application

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The unit has steady orders in term and suppliers that deliver within a day, so JIT and cell production suit it well and would cut stock and waste. The weaker point is kaizen, which relies on staff who know the job well, whereas most of the 12 staff are pupils who stay for one term. Low demand in holidays means that the lack of spare capacity matters little. Training and re-arranging the sewing room cost money and time, but the unit is small. On balance the unit should adopt JIT and cell production, and use a simple monthly kaizen meeting where the permanent staff record the pupils' suggestions so they are not lost each term.

parts.explanation: Uses the case facts - steady orders, reliable suppliers, short-stay staff - to judge.
hints: Compare the unit's conditions with the conditions that make lean production work.

explanation: JIT and cell suit the unit; kaizen is harder with short-stay staff; a justified judgement is needed.
hints: Use the facts in the extract about orders, suppliers and staff.
